Loop Analysis and Operation Counting

Data Structures and Algorithms · Chapter 3 · English review draft · 20 fully worked problems

1. Boundary, prerequisites, and selected written courses

A runtime label is the final line of an analysis, not its first line. This chapter begins with an executable control-flow description, identifies the charged operation, counts how often it is reached, and only then simplifies the result. It covers sequential and nested nonrecursive loops, fixed and data-dependent bounds, arithmetic/geometric/harmonic sums, early exits, nonuniform body costs, termination, and multiple independent size parameters. Recurrence solving, amortized data-structure methods, and full analyses of particular sorting algorithms are scheduled separately. We may use a small insertion-style loop here to teach input-dependent iteration counts, without treating this as the sorting chapter.

Prerequisites are the computation model and input-size contract from Chapter 1, asymptotic notation from Chapter 2, elementary sums, logarithms, and induction. Four written university texts were read in their relevant portions: MIT 6.006 Lecture 1, Stanford CS161 Fall 2014 Lecture 1, Princeton COS226 Analysis of Algorithms, and Berkeley CS61B's two Asymptotics study guides. MIT contributes a dependent-loop cost and explicit array-allocation charge; Stanford distinguishes best from worst shifting counts; Princeton develops frequency-by-cost and exact pair/triple counting; Berkeley stresses that nesting alone does not determine order. The source audit records page-level comparisons and access limits. Every code fragment, solved problem, and figure below is independently written, even when its reasoning type was prompted by one of these texts.

2. A disciplined operation-counting protocol

2.1 Fix the contract before counting

Assume that n is a nonnegative integer supplied in an addressable word, that loop counters and addresses fit in words, and that an arithmetic operation on a bounded number of such words costs one abstract step. An operation on an arbitrary-precision integer may require more; a library call, string append, array initialization, or print statement is not automatically a unit-cost primitive. We write tick() for one specified constant-cost action with no visible output. If the intended cost model is comparison count, an assignment or test may be irrelevant to the reported comparison count while still contributing to full running time. We state which quantity is being measured.

For exact iteration counts, the pseudocode for i = a, a+d, … while i < b means: initialize i=a once; check the guard before each body execution; execute the body if true; then add fixed d>0. The bound b is evaluated at each guard unless the fragment explicitly caches it. For simple constant-cost bounds this changes only a constant factor. A normal loop with q body executions performs q+1 guard evaluations, including the final false one, and q updates. A break, exception, nonlocal return, or short-circuit condition changes this exact pattern. If a guard itself scans an array, multiplying q+1 by unit cost is wrong.

The cost ledger is conceptually

T(x) = ∑operation types a frequencya(x) · costa(x).

The frequency may depend on the instance x, not just its size. The cost may depend on operand length, allocation size, or output length. For a fixed word-RAM primitive it is bounded by a constant; for a call that constructs k characters, it generally is not. To prove T∈Θ(F), give both a uniform upper bound and a valid lower bound on the quantity being classified. An exact count of a chosen tick() may be different from the complete runtime because guard and update work remains.

2.2 Four stages of an analysis

  1. Validate control flow. Establish that each loop terminates for the stated domain and that arithmetic does not wrap. A nonterminating loop has no finite runtime bound under that semantics.
  2. Describe the iteration set. For nested loops write the set of index tuples on which the operation executes. A bound depending on an outer index creates a region, not a rectangular product.
  3. Count or bound that set. Use an exact finite sum when practical; otherwise provide upper and lower sums or a grouping argument. Keep overhead operations in the ledger.
  4. Name the claim. Say whether the result is an exact operation count, an O upper bound for every input, a Θ bound for every input, or a worst-case/best-case bound with an input family that witnesses it. Big-O alone is never evidence for a matching Ω.

2.3 Elementary loop signatures

Under the fixed-width, nonoverflow assumption, i = 0; while i < n: tick(); i += 1 executes tick() exactly n times and tests its guard n+1 times. If the increment is d>0, the body count is ⌈n/d⌉ for n≥0 when starting at zero and using < n. For a loop i = 1; while i < n: tick(); i *= 2, the visited positive values are 1,2,4,…,2q−1; for n≥1, the body executes ⌈log2n⌉ times. Starting this multiplicative loop at i=0 leaves i at zero forever when n>0. Calling that loop logarithmic would conceal a termination error.

Likewise, i = n; while i > 0: tick(); i //= 2 visits n,⌊n/2⌋,…,1. For n≥1, the count is ⌊log2n⌋+1; for n=0, it is zero. The exact floor is useful when the task asks for a count, while Θ(log(n+1)) describes its growth uniformly over nonnegative n only after interpreting the zero case and adding a constant if a positive whole-program cost is measured.

3. The sums that actually arise from loops

3.1 Arithmetic, power, and geometric sums

The dependent pair loop for i = 0,…,n−1; for j = 0,…,i−1: tick() has i inner executions on outer pass i. Its exact count is

∑i=0n−1 i = n(n−1)/2 = C(n,2).

To derive the identity without memorization, pair the first and last terms: 0+(n−1)=n−1, 1+(n−2)=n−1, and so on, or use induction on n. For n≥2, this is Θ(n2). The exact n=0,1 counts are zero; an asymptotic label does not change that.

For fixed real p≥0, the positive sum Sp(n)=∑i=1nip is Θ(np+1). The upper bound is n·np. At least ⌈n/2⌉ terms have i≥n/2, yielding Sp(n)≥(n/2)(n/2)p=np+1/2p+1. These are uniform witnesses for fixed p. If p itself grows with n, the constants in this proof change, so one must revisit the claim.

For r>1 and integer m≥0, multiplying G=1+r+⋯+rm by r and subtracting gives (r−1)G=rm+1−1. Hence

∑k=0mrk = (rm+1−1)/(r−1) ∈ Θ(rm), for fixed r>1.

The number of terms is m+1, but the sum of their work is dominated by the final term. In contrast, a loop that does exactly one tick() at each of those m+1 values costs Θ(m+1). Always distinguish work per iteration from number of iterations. For a decreasing geometric sum n+n/2+n/4+⋯, the full infinite upper bound is 2n and the first term gives an n lower bound; any finite prefix that includes the first term is therefore Θ(n).

3.2 Harmonic sums and integer multiples

The harmonic number Hn=∑i=1n1/i is Θ(log n) for n≥2. Because 1/x decreases, comparison with unit-width rectangles gives

ln(n+1) ≤ Hn ≤ 1+ln n.

Both inequalities are easy to check: 1/i≥∫ii+1dx/x and, for i≥2, 1/i≤∫i−1idx/x. The integral estimates the sum's growth; it is not an exact replacement for discrete counting.

If an outer index i=1,…,n controls an inner loop over positive multiples i,2i,…≤n, its exact body count is ⌊n/i⌋. The total D(n)=∑i=1n⌊n/i⌋ satisfies nHn−n<D(n)≤nHn by x−1<⌊x⌋≤x. A clean lower bound avoids subtraction of a potentially large error term: ⌊n/i⌋≥n/(2i) whenever i≤n (since n/i≥1 and ⌊x⌋≥x/2 for x≥1). Therefore D(n)≥(n/2)Hn, and the tight result is D(n)∈Θ(n log n).

3.3 Exact counts versus integrals and geometry

For an increasing nonnegative function f, ∫0nf(x)dx≤∑i=1nf(i)≤∫1n+1f(x)dx. For a decreasing nonnegative function the rectangle inequalities reverse appropriately. This is a bound derived from monotonicity, not a license to replace every finite sum with an integral or claim its leading constant without proof. For example, the infinite discrete sum ∑k=0∞2−k=2, whereas ∫0∞2−xdx=1/ln2; the values differ. Exact arithmetic/geometric formulas are preferable when available.

The index region also provides a geometric check. The condition 0≤j<i<n occupies the strict lower triangle of an n×n integer grid. Each unordered pair of distinct indices corresponds to exactly one point in that triangle; hence the exact count is C(n,2). Strictly ordered triples 0≤i<j<k<n correspond similarly to three-element index subsets, so their exact count is C(n,3)=n(n−1)(n−2)/6. For fixed tuple length r, the same argument yields C(n,r)∈Θ(nr). Index constraints, not the visible number of for keywords, determine the region.

4. From loop syntax to an index region

4.1 Rectangles, triangles, and variable step sizes

If two independent loops each run exactly n times and their joint body has constant cost, their iteration set is a rectangle with n2 points. If the inner limit is the outer index, the set is a triangle, and the count is a sum. If the inner counter is multiplied, the number of its visits depends logarithmically on the current outer bound. This distinction is more reliable than counting the number of nested for statements.

Consider for i=1..n: for j=1; j<=i; j*=2: tick(). On pass i, the permitted values are 1,2,4,…,2⌊log2i⌋, so the exact count is ⌊log2i⌋+1. Summing yields ∑i=1n(⌊log2i⌋+1). Every summand is at most ⌊log2n⌋+1, giving an O(n log(n+1)) upper bound. For at least ⌈n/2⌉ values, i≥n/2, and each of those summands is Ω(log n) for sufficiently large n. The result is Θ(n log n). Here and below, a notation such as Θ(n log n) is an asymptotic statement for large positive n; exact formulas settle small inputs.

Change the loops to i=1; while i<=n: for j=1..i: tick(); i*=2. The outer values are powers of two, but the inner work grows with them. For m=⌊log2n⌋, the count is 1+2+⋯+2m=2m+1−1. Because 2m≤n<2m+1, the count lies between n and 2n−1 up to endpoint conventions. It is Θ(n), even though the inner loop sometimes runs many times and the outer loop has Θ(log n) passes. Multiplication of the two maximum bounds would count impossible index pairs.

Another useful dependency is for i=1..n: for j=i; j<=n; j+=i: tick(). The inner values are positive multiples of i, so the result is the divisor sum D(n)=∑⌊n/i⌋=Θ(n log n) derived above. If the step changes from i to a fixed positive constant, the count changes to a quadratic triangular sum. The update rule is as important as the loop limit.

4.2 Reverse multiplicative dependency

For for i=1..n: j=i; while j<=n: tick(); j*=2, the inner values are i,2i,4i,…. Count the same execution pairs by their number of doublings k. At level k, the valid starting indices satisfy i≤⌊n/2k⌋. Therefore the exact count is

∑k=0⌊log2n⌋⌊n/2k⌋, for n≥1.

The first term is n; the entire sum is at most 2n. Thus the result is Θ(n). An alternative expression, ∑i=1n(⌊log2(n/i)⌋+1), looks superficially like n log n because some early i produce logarithmic inner counts. The exchange of summation order exposes the actual geometry: only a shrinking fraction of starts can survive many doublings. Interchanging the order is valid because the set of execution pairs is finite and all terms are nonnegative.

4.3 Polynomially shaped limits

The loop for i=1..n: for j=1; j*j<=i; j++: tick() has exactly ⌊√i⌋ inner visits on pass i, assuming the multiplication in the guard is well-defined without overflow. Since ∑i=1n√i∈Θ(n3/2) by the power-sum argument, the floor does not change the order: for i≥1, ⌊√i⌋≥√i/2. The result is Θ(n3/2). This is not an integer exponent forced by the number of loops.

The converse shape is for i=1..n: for j=1; j<=i*i; j++: tick(), which executes ∑i2=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6∈Θ(n3) times, provided i2 fits the model. For a general fixed p≥0, ∑ip∈Θ(np+1). Do not apply this fixed-exponent theorem when p=p(n) varies with input size.

4.4 Supermultiplicative counters and their domain

With arbitrary-precision arithmetic, i=2; while i<n: tick(); i=i*i visits 2,4,16,256,…,22k. After k updates the value is 22k, proved by induction: squaring doubles the outer exponent. The body count for n>2 is the smallest integer q≥0 for which 22q≥n; hence it is ⌈log2log2n⌉. For n≤2, the count is zero. A fixed-width implementation can overflow and cease to increase, so the mathematical bound assumes checked arithmetic or a large-enough integer type. Moreover, the bit cost of squaring ever-growing big integers is not constant. The result counts loop visits under a unit-cost arithmetic model, not total bit operations.

5. Input-dependent control flow and tight bounds

5.1 Early return: separate the path from the input size

Suppose a scan checks each of n items and returns on the first match. On an instance with first match at position k, using one-based positions, the equality comparison runs exactly k times. If no item matches it runs exactly n times. The best case for nonempty arrays is Θ(1); the worst is Θ(n), witnessed by a no-match array. An O(n) bound holds for every input but does not assert that every input costs Θ(n). For a probabilistic expected value one must specify a probability distribution for the match position and absent case; no expected bound follows from best and worst alone.

The same distinction applies to a pair search that compares element pairs until a duplicate is found. It has at most C(n,2) pair comparisons. If the domain permits n distinct values, an all-distinct input forces all comparisons and proves a quadratic worst case. If the domain contains fewer than n possible values, that particular witness is impossible, and the actual worst case needs a new argument. Conditions on the input domain can change a lower-bound proof even when the pseudocode does not change.

5.2 Insertion-style shifting and inversion counts

Consider the following stable ascending insertion fragment. Assume distinct keys for the first exact-count argument and count successful shifts of array entries, leaving comparisons, copying, and header overhead as separate operations.

for i = 1, ..., n-1:
    key = A[i]
    j = i-1
    while j >= 0 and A[j] > key:
        A[j+1] = A[j]       # one successful shift
        j -= 1
    A[j+1] = key

On pass i, the prefix A[0..i−1] is sorted. Each earlier key greater than key shifts once, so the pass makes exactly as many shifts as there are earlier greater keys. Summed over all passes, the number of successful shifts is the original array's inversion count, I(A)=|{(p,q):0≤p<q<n, A[p]>A[q]}|. Why does each inversion correspond to one shift? When the later member at q is inserted, each greater earlier member must move right past it exactly once, and no other element shifts past it. Equality is excluded because the strict > guard maintains stability.

For sorted ascending input, I(A)=0; for strictly descending input, I(A)=C(n,2). Full runtime is nevertheless Θ(n+I(A)) in the unit-cost model: the outer loop and one initial or terminal condition evaluation per pass contribute Θ(n); each successful shift contributes a constant amount of additional work. More specifically, the first guard operand j>=0 is evaluated once per successful shift and once more at the end of each pass. The second comparison A[j]>key is skipped by short-circuit evaluation when j<0; therefore it need not equal shifts plus outer passes. For ascending input it is n−1; for strictly descending input it is C(n,2), because every pass ends at j<0 without a final key comparison. This detail matters when a question asks for key comparisons, not generic runtime. Thus best-case full runtime is Θ(n) and worst-case full runtime is Θ(n2).

5.3 Branch costs, compound guards, and lower-bound witnesses

If a branch executes a constant-cost action on one input and a length-n scan on another, counting branch frequency without identifying the chosen path cannot yield a fixed cost per pass. Write an indicator or partition the input set: T(x)=Tbase(x)+1branch(x)·Tscan(x). To claim a worst-case lower bound, exhibit an input family that makes the costly branch feasible on sufficiently many passes. A bound obtained by replacing every branch with its maximum cost gives a valid upper bound but may be loose if those maxima cannot occur together.

For while P(i) and Q(i): ..., short-circuit semantics evaluate Q(i) only if P(i) is true. A normal terminating loop checks P once beyond the last body pass. A break from inside the body avoids that final header check. If P and Q have different costs, a single “number of condition checks” is ambiguous. State which predicate, and whether the terminating check is included.

6. Work beyond body-iteration counts

6.1 A nonconstant body changes the sum

The exact iteration set may be easy while the body is expensive. If pass i calls a routine costing Θ(i) for every relevant input, n outer passes cost ∑i=1nΘ(i)=Θ(n2). The last equality relies on positive uniform upper and lower constants for the calls. If the routine merely costs O(i), the sum only yields O(n2); the routine could actually take constant time on the instances reaching it.

For an inner geometric loop, a constant-time tick() gives logarithmic work per outer pass, while a call that writes j characters at the visited value j gives work 1+2+4+⋯+2⌊log2i⌋=Θ(i) on pass i. Summed over i=1,…,n, this becomes Θ(n2), not Θ(n log n). Output length alone provides a lower bound if every generated character must be written. A language-level concatenation may additionally copy previous content, so its cost requires an explicit string representation.

6.2 Exact headers, auxiliary memory, and multiple dimensions

For for i=0; i<n; i++ with a simple guard and no abnormal exit, body count is n, guard count n+1, and increment count n. For nested loops with outer i=0,…,n−1 and inner j=0,…,i−1, inner body count is C(n,2), but inner guard count is ∑i=0n−1(i+1)=C(n,2)+n. Reporting the body count as the exact runtime silently drops those tests. All terms still yield Θ(n2) total time for sufficiently large n when primitive costs are fixed and positive.

Space has a separate accounting. A scan over an existing array may use O(1) auxiliary words even though it takes Θ(n) time; constructing an array of n words has Θ(n) output or auxiliary storage depending on convention. A nested loop does not, by itself, require nested storage.

For dimensions m and n, a rectangular traversal costs Θ(mn) if it actually visits every cell at constant cost. It is generally invalid to write Θ(n2) unless one has established m∈Θ(n). If a separate preprocessing phase takes Θ(m+n), total time is Θ(mn+m+n) for independent nonnegative dimensions; do not discard linear terms when one dimension may be zero. A one-variable asymptotic conclusion always rests on a relation among the size parameters.

6.3 Termination is a precondition to runtime analysis

A loop variant is a nonnegative integer expression that strictly decreases on each iteration; it proves termination if every body step preserves the domain and cannot reset the variant. For i=n; while i>0: i//=2, the positive integer i decreases when i≥2 and becomes zero from one, so termination follows. For i=0; while i<n: i*=2, the value stays zero for n>0, so no such progress proof exists and the loop does not terminate. For fixed-width signed arithmetic, even i*=2 from one may overflow; bounds derived from monotone mathematical integers cannot simply be transferred to a wrapping implementation. For unbounded integers, iteration count alone ignores bit-complexity. State which model the question asks about before simplifying.

7. Fully worked problems

The fragments below are original teaching exercises. Problems 1–5 develop Princeton's exact-frequency and MIT's dependent-loop reasoning; Problems 6–12 extend Berkeley's arithmetic-versus-geometric patterns; Problems 13–17 develop Stanford's input-dependent counting and cost-model cautions; the final problems integrate the four sources. Unless stated otherwise, n is a nonnegative integer, tick() has constant positive cost, arithmetic does not overflow, and a displayed count concerns calls to tick() rather than every machine instruction.

Problem 1. The extra guard test

Question. For i=0; while i<n: tick(); i++, count body calls, guard evaluations, and increments, including n=0. If each costs respectively cb, cg, cu and initialization costs c0, give the exact modeled cost.

Solution. Body values are 0,…,n−1, exactly n of them. Each successful guard is followed by one body and one increment, and one additional false guard ends the loop. Thus body and increment counts are n and guard count is n+1. The cost is c0+(n+1)cg+n(cb+cu). At n=0 this leaves initialization and one false test, which is why replacing exact runtime by zero is wrong even though tick() runs zero times.

Problem 2. Inclusive and exclusive endpoints

Question. Compare the tick() counts for j=0; j<n; j+=3 and j=0; j<=n; j+=3.

Solution. The first executes at nonnegative multiples of three strictly below n. For n=0 it executes zero times; in general its count is ⌈n/3⌉. The second includes zero and every multiple at most n, so its count is ⌊n/3⌋+1. For n=6, the first gives two visits (0,3), while the second gives three (0,3,6). For n=7, both give three (0,3,6). A one-symbol guard change can alter exact counts without changing the Θ(n) class.

Problem 3. Triangular body and header counts

Question. For for i=0..n−1: for j=0..i−1: tick(), count inner body calls and inner guard evaluations under the header convention of Section 2.

Solution. At outer value i, the inner body runs i times and checks its guard i+1 times, even for i=0. Summing gives ∑i=C(n,2) bodies and ∑(i+1)=C(n,2)+n=n(n+1)/2 inner guard checks. With simple constant-cost operations, full time is Θ(n2) for large n. The exact inner body count at n=0 and n=1 is zero, whereas the inner guard count at n=1 is one.

Problem 4. Strictly ordered triples

Question. Count tick() in for i=0..n−1: for j=i+1..n−1: for k=j+1..n−1: tick().

Solution. Each execution has 0≤i<j<k<n. Choosing any three distinct indices uniquely orders them into one such triple, so the exact count is C(n,3)=n(n−1)(n−2)/6. If n<3, it is zero. If n≥3, the cubic leading term yields Θ(n3). Multiplying three n-sized maxima would give an upper bound but incorrectly claim exactly n3 visits and count many invalid tuples.

Problem 5. A quadratic body hidden in linear syntax

Question. An outer loop runs at i=1,…,n. On pass i, a specified subroutine performs exactly 2i+1 constant-cost operations. Find the exact subroutine work and tight asymptotic order.

Solution. Sum work, not just outer visits: ∑(2i+1)=2[n(n+1)/2]+n=n2+2n. Hence it is Θ(n2). If the subroutine's stated count were merely an upper bound, this would prove only O(n2); the equality here supplies the matching lower bound.

Problem 6. Multiplicative inner loop

Question. Count tick() for for i=1..n: j=1; while j<=i: tick(); j*=2, and prove a tight order.

Solution. For each positive i, powers 2k≤i correspond to k=0,…,⌊log2i⌋, so the exact sum is ∑i=1n(⌊log2i⌋+1). It is at most n(⌊log2n⌋+1). The indices i≥⌈n/2⌉ form at least half the outer passes and each costs at least ⌊log2(n/2)⌋+1 for sufficiently large n. Therefore the lower and upper bounds match at Θ(n log n). This is a sum of logarithms, not a product inferred solely from nesting.

Problem 7. Geometric outer, linear inner

Question. For i=1; while i<=n: for j=1..i: tick(); i*=2, give an exact formula and asymptotic order for n≥1.

Solution. Let m=⌊log2n⌋. The outer values are 20,…,2m; the inner body runs that many times on each pass. The exact count is 2m+1−1. Since 2m≤n<2m+1, the count is greater than or equal to n? When n=6, it is seven, but when n=7, it is seven. Indeed 2m+1−1≥n for every integer n in the interval, while 2m+1−1<2n. Thus it is Θ(n). The precise interval check matters; saying “last term equals n” would be false unless n is a power of two.

Problem 8. Multiples and harmonic work

Question. Count tick() for for i=1..n: for j=i; j<=n; j+=i: tick() and show tight growth.

Solution. At a fixed i, j takes i,2i,…,⌊n/i⌋i, so the exact count is D(n)=∑i=1n⌊n/i⌋. Since n/i≥1, (n/2i)≤⌊n/i⌋≤n/i. Summing gives (n/2)Hn≤D(n)≤nHn. As Hn∈Θ(log n) for large n, the result is Θ(n log n). Replacing every inner length by n produces only a loose quadratic upper bound.

Problem 9. Doubling from each starting index

Question. Analyze for i=1..n: j=i; while j<=n: tick(); j*=2.

Solution. A body execution is identified by a starting index i and doubling count k≥0 satisfying 2ki≤n. For fixed k, exactly ⌊n/2k⌋ starts work. Thus the exact count is ∑k=0⌊log2n⌋⌊n/2k⌋. Its first term is n, and the whole sum is below 2n. It is Θ(n). This is a useful counterexample to the reflex “an outer linear loop containing a logarithmic loop must be n log n”; the logarithmic maximum occurs for only the smallest starts.

Problem 10. Square-root boundary

Question. For for i=1..n: j=1; while j*j<=i: tick(); j++, give an exact sum and tight order.

Solution. Exactly ⌊√i⌋ positive integers satisfy j2≤i. The total is ∑⌊√i⌋. Since √i/2≤⌊√i⌋≤√i for i≥1, comparison with the power sum gives Θ(n3/2). A finite-width program should test j <= i // j or use checked multiplication to avoid overflow in j*j; the asymptotic claim assumes a mathematically correct guard.

Problem 11. A squared inner bound

Question. Analyze for i=1..n: for j=1..i*i: tick().

Solution. Pass i executes i2 times. The exact count is ∑i=1ni2=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, a cubic polynomial with positive leading coefficient. Thus it is Θ(n3). Counting two loop headers and guessing Θ(n2) misses the squared bound; conversely, replacing each inner count by n2 yields a valid but non-exact upper bound of n3.

Problem 12. A logarithm of a logarithm

Question. For i=2; while i<n: tick(); i=i*i, give the exact body count for n=2,3,4,5,17 and a general formula.

Solution. The visited values begin 2,4,16,256. Counts are respectively 0,1,1,2,3: at n=17, 2, 4, and 16 pass the strict guard. After q updates the value is 22q. Therefore the number of bodies is the least q≥0 with 22q≥n, which is max(0,⌈log2log2n⌉) for n≥2. At n=2 the expression is zero. Under unit-cost squaring it grows as Θ(log log n) for sufficiently large n; bit complexity is a different question.

Problem 13. A search with three distinct claims

Question. A scan returns when A[i]==target. State the number of equality comparisons if the first match is at zero-based index k, if absent, and the best and worst full-time classes for nonempty arrays.

Solution. Reaching index k requires failed checks at 0,…,k−1 and one successful check, so comparisons equal k+1. Absence requires n comparisons. A match at index zero witnesses Θ(1) best-case time; an absent target witnesses Θ(n) worst-case time. An O(n) all-input upper bound is correct, but an Ω(n) all-input lower bound is false. For n=0, the equality count is zero although loop setup still costs a constant amount.

Problem 14. Pair search and witness feasibility

Question. A routine compares each pair (i,j) with i<j until it finds equal values. Give an all-input upper bound and a condition making it a tight worst-case bound.

Solution. Every pair is examined at most once, so comparisons are at most C(n,2), giving O(n2). If the input domain contains at least n distinct values, choose an all-distinct array. The routine then cannot exit early and performs exactly C(n,2) comparisons, proving worst-case Θ(n2). If fewer than n distinct values exist, that lower-bound witness cannot be used; a pigeonhole guarantee of some duplicate does not tell us where the routine will find it. The order of pair examination and domain size then require a separate worst-case analysis.

Problem 15. Shifts are inversions; comparisons are not identical

Question. Apply the insertion fragment of Section 5 to arrays [1,2,3,4] and [4,3,2,1]. Count successful shifts and key comparisons, and state full-time orders on size-n sorted and reverse-sorted families.

Solution. Sorted input has no inversion, hence zero shifts. Each of its three passes checks A[j] > key once and fails, giving three key comparisons. Reverse-sorted input has C(4,2)=6 inversions and six shifts. On passes i=1,2,3, all i earlier elements are greater than the key, so there are 1+2+3=6 key comparisons; the guard ends when j becomes negative, so there is no extra failed key comparison. At general size, sorted full time is Θ(n) from loop overhead, reverse-sorted full time is Θ(n2) from the inversion sum. For mixed input, shift count is exactly I(A), but key-comparison count also depends on how each pass stops.

Problem 16. A costly body under a geometric schedule

Question. For each i=1,…,n, visit j=1,2,4,…≤i and write exactly j characters. Bound the total number of characters written.

Solution. Let m=⌊log2i⌋. The pass writes 1+2+⋯+2m=2m+1−1 characters. This lies between i and 2i, as in Problem 7. Summing over i=1,…,n gives a total between n(n+1)/2 and n(n+1), hence Θ(n2) output characters and at least that much work in any model that physically emits them. Counting only the inner visits would suggest Θ(n log n) and undercount the variable-size write.

Problem 17. A branch whose maximum cannot be multiplied blindly

Question. On each pass i=1,…,n, the program executes a scan of length i only if a predicate P(i,x) holds; otherwise it performs one unit operation. What can be concluded without information about P? What changes if there is an input family for which it holds on every pass?

Solution. With a constant-cost predicate, each pass costs at least a constant and at most O(i), so every input has Ω(n) and O(n2) total time. No single all-input Θ(n2) claim follows: a predicate false on every pass gives Θ(n). If some feasible input family makes the predicate true on every pass, its scan work is ∑i=Θ(n2), proving quadratic worst-case time. If predicate evaluation itself is costly, its cost must be added and these conclusions revisited.

Problem 18. Two independent dimensions

Question. An algorithm initializes arrays of lengths m and n, then visits all m·n pairs once. Under unit word initialization and per-pair work, give the tight time for independent nonnegative m,n.

Solution. Initialization costs Θ(m+n); the rectangular traversal costs Θ(mn). Their sum is Θ(m+n+mn) when constants remain uniformly positive. Retaining all terms handles m=0 or n=0, where the pair work vanishes. If both dimensions are known to be Θ(k), then the same expression reduces to Θ(k2); without that relation, Θ(n2) is unjustified.

Problem 19. Zero-start doubling is not logarithmic

Question. Analyze i=0; while i<n: tick(); i*=2 for n=0 and n>0. Give a repair that does Θ(log n) visits for growing n.

Solution. At n=0, the guard is false immediately and tick() is never called. At n>0, zero satisfies the guard, and doubling keeps it zero, so the loop does not terminate. Starting at one repairs progress: i=1; while i<n: tick(); i*=2 makes exactly ⌈log2n⌉ visits for n≥1, which is Θ(log n) for sufficiently large n. A finite-width language still needs an overflow-safe stopping rule for very large bounds.

Problem 20. Integrals bound rather than exactly count

Question. An analyst replaces ∑k=0m2k by ∫0m2xdx and reports the latter as the exact number of operations. Identify the error and provide the correct count.

Solution. The operations occur at discrete integer values, so their exact number is the geometric sum 2m+1−1. The integral equals (2m−1)/ln2, a different value. Both have Θ(2m) growth for large m, but a growth estimate is not an exact count. For m=0, the sum is one and the integral is zero, an immediate counterexample to the asserted equality. Use finite-sum identities for exact answers and monotonicity-aware integral comparisons for bounds.

8. High-yield review: complete decisions and common traps

This sheet is for recall after the derivations and problems. It is deliberately concise, but each statement names the condition that makes it valid.

  1. Declare the size and model. Name the input parameter, which operations are charged, whether words have bounded width, and whether a called routine or output statement has nonconstant cost. Without these, “the time is logarithmic” has no precise referent.
  2. Prove progress first. A multiplicative update from zero can loop forever. Squaring or doubling may overflow in fixed-width arithmetic. A finite asymptotic bound applies only after termination and arithmetic semantics are fixed.
  3. Separate exact count from order. tick() calls, guard checks, updates, and full runtime are different quantities. A normal loop with q body visits has q+1 simple-guard checks; a break may remove the final check.
  4. Write the iteration set. For nested loops, specify the valid index tuples. Independent limits form a rectangle; a bound depending on an outer index forms another region and must be summed.
  5. Arithmetic triangle. 0≤j&lt;i&lt;n gives exactly C(n,2)=n(n−1)/2 body visits. The count is zero for n=0,1 and quadratic asymptotically.
  6. Ordered triples. 0≤i&lt;j&lt;k&lt;n gives exactly C(n,3) visits; three loop headers alone do not imply this count.
  7. Fixed positive step. Starting at zero, repeatedly adding d>0 while j<n gives ⌈n/d⌉ body visits. Changing < to <= changes the exact endpoint count.
  8. Powers of two. Starting at one and doubling while j<=i gives ⌊log2i⌋+1 visits for i≥1. With <i, it gives ⌈log2i⌉. State the guard before using either formula.
  9. Linear outer, geometric inner. ∑i=1n(⌊log2i⌋+1)=Θ(n log n). A constant fraction of outer passes supplies the lower bound.
  10. Geometric outer, linear inner. If the outer indices double and pass i costs i, then total work is a geometric sum Θ(n), not Θ(n log n).
  11. Multiples. Inner values i,2i,…≤n produce ⌊n/i⌋ visits. Summed over i=1,…,n, the order is Θ(n log n) by comparison with nHn.
  12. Doubling from each start. Inner values i,2i,…≤n for every start i yield ∑k≥0⌊n/2k⌋=Θ(n). Recount by doubling depth when a sum of logarithms looks misleading.
  13. Power sums. For fixed p≥0, ∑i=1nip=Θ(np+1). A growing exponent requires a new argument.
  14. Square-root bound. j*j<=i with positive consecutive j gives ⌊√i⌋ visits; summing over i≤n gives Θ(n3/2) if the guard does not overflow.
  15. Geometric work is not geometric visit count. A loop visiting 1,2,4,…,2m has m+1 visits. If visit 2k costs that many operations, work is 2m+1−1.
  16. Harmonic comparison. ln(n+1)≤Hn≤1+ln n. Integral comparison establishes bounds, not an equality between a finite sum and an integral.
  17. Prove both sides of a tight bound. Summing maxima gives an upper bound. To claim worst-case Θ(F(n)), exhibit feasible inputs causing Ω(F(n)) work. An early return may make every ordinary input cheaper.
  18. State best, worst, or per-instance. A search can be Θ(1) best case and Θ(n) worst case. A single unqualified Θ(n) claim does not describe both.
  19. Insertion-style shifts. With strict > and stable insertion, successful shifts equal the original inversion count. Full time includes Θ(n) overhead and is Θ(n+I(A)) under the unit-cost model. Key comparisons are not automatically identical to shifts because the final guard can fail or short-circuit.
  20. Compound guards. In P and Q, a false P prevents evaluation of Q. Count expensive subconditions separately; do not assign one unit to a guard that scans data.
  21. Variable body cost. If work on pass i is Θ(f(i)) with uniform positive constants, total work is Θ(∑f(i)). An O(f(i)) promise only gives an upper bound when summed.
  22. Independent dimensions. Preserve m and n in a rectangular traversal: Θ(mn). Initialization may add Θ(m+n); retain it when either dimension may be zero.
  23. Check small values. Evaluate n=0,1,2 and values immediately around a power of two. These detect missing guard checks, floor/ceiling mistakes, and false claims of exact equality.
  24. Five-step exam procedure. (i) Fix the cost contract and input domain. (ii) Prove termination and list actual visited indices. (iii) Write an exact sum or finite set of visits. (iv) Bound it above and below, identifying a witness if the claim is worst-case. (v) Report the precise quantity and qualification: exact body count, all-input bound, best case, worst case, or expected case under a specified distribution.

The source audit distinguishes portions actually read from candidates only screened. The exercises are independently worded and solved rather than copied from course handouts. This chapter covers the named nonrecursive loop patterns and their identified boundary cases; it does not claim to enumerate every program, every university exercise, or every unseen examination problem. Compiler behavior, input/output costs, arbitrary-precision arithmetic, concurrency, caches, and distribution-dependent expected cases require their own models. A strong result on future examination questions depends on practice and verified transfer of these methods, not a literal guarantee of 100% performance.
